handoff.purpose: Implement unresolved import detection, imports_resolve check, baseline check tuple, run_checks fail-closed runner, and with_markers policy helper.

symbols.name: unresolved_first_party_imports
symbols.note: Static AST walk; reports missing first-party modules and names; returns deduplicated, order-preserving list.

symbols.name: imports_resolve
symbols.note: Check wrapper; returns empty string when imports resolve; otherwise formatted refusal with cap.

symbols.name: BASELINE
symbols.note: Tuple of checks ordered: not_truncated, no_elision, parses, not_substituted, imports_resolve.

symbols.name: run_checks
symbols.note: Runs baseline plus extra checks; fail-closed on exception; returns first non-empty reason.

symbols.name: with_markers
symbols.note: Returns a new CheckPolicy with replaced elision_markers.

claims.text: First-party imports in ``content`` that name nothing in the tree.
claims.why: Function performs static AST walk and checks first-party roots against module paths and exports; returns list of missing modules/names.

claims.text: MEASURED 2026-07-30. Twenty agents wrote test modules against source files they were given, and three of seven imported things that do not exist: ``daedalus.linting`` (it is ``daedalus.gui.lint``), ``ShiftManager`` from ``daedalus.shift`` (the class is ``Shift``), and ``daedalus.wiki_vault`` (it is ``daedalus.wiki.vault``). All three are valid Python, so a syntax gate passes them, and all three reported ``status: done``.
claims.why: Claims about external measurements and specific historical examples; not verifiable from this code chunk.

claims.text: The check is STATIC on purpose. Importing the file to find out whether its imports resolve would execute module-level code from an untrusted lane -- the one thing this repository refuses to do to decide whether to trust something.
claims.why: Function uses ast.parse and ast.walk; no import statements are executed.

claims.text: only first-party roots are judged;
claims.why: Both Import and ImportFrom branches check alias.name.split('.')[0] or node.module.split('.')[0] against roots.

claims.text: a missing MODULE is reported, since that cannot be a re-export;
claims.why: When _module_path returns None for the module, appends 'module does not exist'.

claims.text: a missing NAME is reported only when the module has no star-import and no module-level ``__getattr__``.
claims.why: _exports returns opaque flag; if opaque, continue skips name checks; star import skipped via alias.name == '*'.

claims.text: a parse failure is a different guard's business
claims.why: Catches SyntaxError, ValueError, RecursionError and returns [].

claims.text: relative imports resolve against a package
claims.why: Skips ImportFrom nodes when node.level is truthy or node.module is None.

claims.text: `from daemon import shift` binds a SUBMODULE, which is perfectly valid and is named nowhere in the package's __init__.py. Measured: without this the check fired on 40 of 223 real files in this repo -- a false-positive rate that would have made the gate useless and, worse, trained everyone to ignore it.
claims.why: The specific measurement is not verifiable from code; the submodule check itself is present.

claims.text: Deduplicated but order-preserving: the same bad import repeated ten times is one problem, and the first occurrence is the one worth naming.
claims.why: Uses list(dict.fromkeys(bad)) to preserve first occurrence order.

claims.text: Checked for CREATED files too -- a brand-new test module against an invented API is exactly the failure this catches, and it has no original to compare against.
claims.why: imports_resolve calls unresolved_first_party_imports on attempt.proposed regardless of file type; no check for existing file.

claims.text: FAIL-CLOSED, and this is the part worth not losing: a check that raises is reported as a refusal naming the crash. The alternative -- letting the exception propagate, or catching it and continuing -- turns a broken guard into a silent permission, which is how a gate ends up passing a file that destroyed a module.
claims.why: try/except around each check call returns a refusal message with exception type and message.

claims.text: A lane may pass ``extra`` to ADD checks. There is deliberately no argument for removing one from the baseline.
claims.why: Function accepts extra iterable and concatenates with BASELINE; no removal parameter exists.

claims.text: ``policy`` with this lane's own elision markers. Convenience only.
claims.why: Returns replace(policy, elision_markers=tuple(markers)); does not modify original.

observations.what: The comment on lines 281-282 ("is not an improvement, and letting it land would break an import for every consumer of the module") is a fragment of a larger explanation; it is not a checkable claim but a rationale.
The comment 'Cheapest first' on line 349 implies an ordering rationale, but the code does not enforce any performance measurement; it is a stated intent.

The docstring of unresolved_first_party_imports says 'a missing NAME is reported only when the module has no star-import and no module-level __getattr__.' The code checks _exports(path) which returns opaque flag; opaque is true if star-import or __getattr__, but this is not directly visible in this chunk; the behavior is delegated to _exports.
The check for submodule existence at line 338-340 uses _module_path(root, f"{node.module}.{alias.name}") to allow `from daemon import shift`; this is a special case that bypasses the name check.

The imports_resolve function caps the number of reported imports at policy.max_named_imports, but the exact semantics of max_named_imports (whether it is a cap on report count or something else) is not defined in this chunk.
The BASELINE tuple ordering is stated as load-bearing in one direction only, but the comment does not specify which direction; the code does not enforce any order.
The fail-closed behavior in run_checks catches all exceptions (except BaseException) and returns a refusal; this is robust but could mask programming errors in the checks themselves.

risks: line 349 | low | 'Cheapest first' comment implies performance ordering, but no mechanism enforces it; if a check is expensive, the order may not be cheapest. | Add a comment or test that measures order cost.
lines 326-329 | low | The opaque flag from _exports is not defined in this chunk; if _exports misclassifies, the name check could be skipped incorrectly. | Inspect _exports implementation.
lines 366-370 | low | max_named_imports semantics are not defined; if it is zero, the function would report nothing even when there are bad imports. | Define and test max_named_imports behavior.

lines 366-373 | medium | run_checks catches all exceptions and returns a refusal; this could hide bugs in the checks themselves, making debugging harder. | Add logging or a test to surface exceptions in development.
